cards.explanation: The answer is Joab son of Zeruiah. He marches out with David's servants and meets Abner's side by the pool of Gibeon. Keep that name handy, friends, because Joab is right in the middle of this whole story. His two brothers are on the field too. I think his day is about to get complicated.

The answer is letting the young men compete before them. Abner says to Joab, “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” That's the whole suggestion, and it comes from Abner, not from Joab. The text doesn't say why he asks, so I won't guess. I do think a contest that starts with the word 'compete' sounds friendlier than what comes next.
The answer is False. Joab agrees to Abner's idea. He replies, “Let them get up…” No pushback and no haggling, just yes. Then the young men get up and are counted off.
The answer is twelve. The young men are counted off, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. Twelve and twelve. I'd have counted twice, just to feel useful.

The answer is False. Nobody clearly wins this one. Each man grabs his opponent by the head and thrusts his sword into his opponent's side, and “…they all fell together.” I think this is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't dress it up. The place gets a name, Helkath-hazzurim, and the battle that follows is the intense part.

The answer is Abner and the men of Israel. They are defeated by the servants of David. The text says the battle that day was intense, so this wasn't a gentle loss. The contest at the pool settled nothing, but the fighting that followed did settle this.

The answer is Abner. Asahel chases him, and the text says he never turns to the right or to the left while he does it. He is one of the three sons of Zeruiah, and the text calls him fleet of foot like a wild gazelle. Out of everyone on that field, he picks Abner and sticks with him.
The answer is True. Asahel chases Abner “…not turning to the right or to the left in his pursuit.” He locks onto one target and keeps going. That one detail matters a lot in the verses ahead.

The answer is to grab one of the young men and take his gear. Abner tells Asahel, “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment for yourself.” That's the offer: pick somebody else and walk away with his gear. Abner is giving Asahel a way out. The text doesn't say why, so I won't guess.
The answer is False. Asahel keeps going. The text says he “…would not stop chasing him.” That's why Abner has to speak up a second time. Same runner, same target.

The answer is Asahel's brother Joab. Abner asks, “How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” So Joab is Asahel's brother, and Abner brings him up in the warning itself. The text doesn't say what Abner is thinking beyond those words. I think he's trying hard to talk Asahel out of this.

The answer is that he pauses at that spot. The text says “…every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died.” Everybody who reached that place stopped. The text doesn't say what any of them were thinking, but I think this is a heavy moment, and a pause fits it.

The answer is that the Benjamites rally to Abner and take a stand on a hill. Joab and Abishai are pursuing Abner, and the Benjamites form a single unit and take their stand atop a hill. His side comes together as one group. Then Abner calls out to Joab.

The answer is that Abner wants Joab to tell the troops to stop chasing their brothers. He calls out, “How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” That's his request: call off the chase. He also asks, “Must the sword devour forever?” The word 'brothers' is his, and I think it says a lot.

The answer is that the troops would have kept chasing until morning. Joab says, “As surely as God lives…” and then, “if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” So he says Abner's plea made the difference. The chase would have gone all night. After that, Joab blows the ram's horn.
The answer is False. Joab blows the ram's horn, and all the troops stop. The text says they “…no longer pursued Israel or continued to fight.” The horn sounds and the fighting stops.

The answer is Mahanaim. Abner and his men march all night through the Arabah, cross the Jordan, march all morning, and arrive at Mahanaim. That's the same place they marched out from at the start (2 Samuel 2:12). They come back where they began. That's a long, tiring way to end up in the same spot.

The answer is True, and the gap is big. David's side is missing Asahel and nineteen others, but they struck down 360 Benjamites who were with Abner. That's a huge difference in numbers. It matches what the text said earlier, that Abner and the men of Israel were defeated.

The answer is Bethlehem. They bury Asahel in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. The text calls it his father's tomb and puts it in Bethlehem. After the burial, Joab and his men march all night. The text tells us this and nothing more about it.
The answer is True. The text says the war between the house of Saul and the house of David “was protracted.” That means it dragged on. Gibeon didn't end it, and the story keeps going.

The answer is that David grows stronger and Saul's house grows weaker. The text says David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. The two sides are moving in opposite directions. The war drags on, but it isn't an even race. And the sons born to David in Hebron come right after that line.
